title: Feeding the Five Thousand
lead: What we have too little of can be enough once we give it to Jesus.
questions: What are my five loaves that Jesus is asking for, the ones I still keep in the basket because “what difference will these make among so many?”
Which “it can’t be done” do I hide behind most often, and how would the matter look if I started from what there is?
Who is the youngest or least significant person in my community whom no one has yet asked what they have in their basket?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Yesterday the boat was sinking; today the bread runs out. Apart from the resurrection, this is the only miracle of Jesus recorded by all four evangelists; the first church decided it could not be left out of any version of the story. It begins with exhaustion: the apostles return from their mission, and Jesus orders a rest in a solitary place. The plan collapses, because the crowd runs along the shore and gets there first. And then comes the sentence worth reading slowly: Jesus “had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” These are words from Moses’ prayer for a successor to lead Israel; God answered that prayer by giving Joshua, and in Greek the name Joshua is Jesus. The answer to Israel’s oldest prayer is standing on the shore, moved with compassion.

Toward evening the disciples suggest sending the people away, and Jesus answers: “You give them something to eat.” Philip does the math: two hundred denarii, eight months’ wages, and still not enough. Andrew brings a boy, along with a comment we know from our own mouths: five barley loaves, the bread of the poor, and two fish, “but what difference will these make among so many?” Jesus doesn’t respond to the arithmetic. He has the people sit down in groups of hundreds and fifties, the way Israel was organized on the way out of Egypt, and for an hour He arranges a random crowd into the formation of a people fed with bread from heaven. It was also the largest shared meal with the unclean in all the Gospels: out in the wilderness no one could perform the ritual washings, and Jesus fed everyone until they were full without asking a single screening question. Twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered, “so that nothing will be wasted”: one for each of those who had said it couldn’t be done.

For this the crowd wanted to make Him king; He withdrew to a mountain. In the whole Gospel of John the word “king” appears sixteen times, and never once from His own lips about Himself. The one title He never used is the very one they will accuse Him of before Pilate. And that sentence comes back to us: “You give them something to eat.” He doesn’t demand what we don’t have. He asks for the five loaves we do have, truly handed over.

Yesterday the boat was sinking. Today, just as the title of our section says, the bread runs out. The story we read today is the only miracle of Jesus recorded by all four evangelists, apart from the resurrection itself. The church of the first generations evidently believed that this one scene must not be left out of any version of the story of Jesus. It’s worth asking what they saw in it.

sections.heading: A Vacation That Fell Through
paragraphs: The scene begins with exhaustion. The apostles return from their first mission on their own, excited and worn out, and there is so much traffic around Jesus that “they did not even have time to eat.” Jesus makes a decision every overworked person should frame and hang on the wall: “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” God doesn’t glorify overwork; He Himself orders a retreat. There is also a second reason for this trip, which Mark mentions a few paragraphs earlier: Herod Antipas has just beheaded John the Baptist and has begun to take an interest in Jesus. The shore they are sailing toward lies outside the border of his jurisdiction. Jesus leads His disciples out of reach of a man who kills prophets.

Except that the plan for rest collapses before the boat reaches the shore. People see where they are heading and run on foot along the lake; the whole geography of this scene fits within an hour’s walk. When Jesus steps ashore, the “solitary place” looks like a mass gathering. And here comes the sentence worth reading this story slowly for: Jesus “had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” That is not a loose metaphor. It is a quotation from the book of Numbers, from the prayer of Moses, who before his death asked God for a successor, “so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd.” God answered by giving the people Joshua. And the name Joshua, in Hebrew Yehoshua, in Greek is Jesus. Mark is quoting the verse in which the plea for a shepherd was once answered by a man bearing the very name of the One who is now looking at the crowd. The answer to Israel’s oldest prayer is standing on the shore, moved with compassion.

It’s worth noticing, too, what Jesus did not do: He didn’t cancel the rest; He postponed it. Right after the feeding, Mark adds that Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, dismissed the crowd Himself and went up the mountain to pray. The crowd’s need was urgent, but the need of tired people didn’t stop existing just because a more urgent one had come along. Anyone who serves others will find more pastoral wisdom in that detail than in many a handbook.

sections.heading: You Give Them Something to Eat
paragraphs: Toward evening the disciples come with a sensible proposal: send them away so they can buy food in the villages. Jesus’ answer must have sounded like a joke: “You give them something to eat.” There is a gentle irony in this command that is easy to miss: these same men have just come back from a mission on which they healed the sick and drove out demons. Faced with disease, they acted with power; faced with a shortage of bread, they immediately switched to the language of accounting. Philip does the math in a flash: “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread,” and two hundred denarii was about eight months of a laborer’s wages. The group’s treasury couldn’t cover even a token snack for a crowd like that. Then Andrew brings a boy, adding at once a caveat we know from our own mouths: “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” Barley bread was the bread of the poor, cheaper than wheat; two fish were a dried snack, not a food supply. The entire provision in this scene is a child’s basket of the cheapest food, presented with the comment “it’s not enough anyway.” Jesus doesn’t answer that comment with a single word. He tells the people to sit down.

sections.heading: In Hundreds and Fifties
paragraphs: Mark remembered the details of this seating: “the green grass,” groups “of hundreds and fifties.” The green grass tells us it was spring; John confirms that the Passover was near. And the division into hundreds and fifties told those people something we have to remind ourselves of: this is how Israel was organized in the wilderness, on the way out of Egypt. It was not just the logistics of distribution, or at least not only that. For one hour a crowd of random people on the grass was arranged into the formation of a people coming out of slavery, fed with bread from heaven. Whoever sat in this scene was sitting in the book of Exodus.

And one more thing, which becomes visible only against the customs of the time: this was the largest shared meal with the unclean that the Gospels record. Out in the wilderness no one had any way to observe the rules about ritual washing, and in a crowd of Galilean villagers many were regarded as permanently unclean. A devout teacher was not supposed to break bread with them. Jesus fed them all at once and didn’t ask anyone a single screening question. He fed them first. He postponed the screening until never.

sections.heading: Twelve Baskets
paragraphs: Mark describes the miracle itself with verbs familiar from every Jewish table: He took, He blessed, He broke, He gave. The same four verbs will come back in the upper room over the bread of the Last Supper and at the table in Emmaus, where it is by them that the disciples recognize the risen Lord; this scene on the grass is the first link in a chain that runs to this day through every Communion table. No special effects; the multiplication happens somewhere between His hands and the hands of the disciples handing out the food. And they “all ate and were satisfied,” five thousand men, and with women and children probably well over ten thousand people. God doesn’t hand out starvation rations; when He feeds, He feeds until people are full. Then comes a command that sounds surprising from the lips of the One who has just created food out of nothing: “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” The One for whom bread costs nothing does not allow it to be wasted. Abundance and respect for crumbs don’t exclude each other; with God they go hand in hand. Twelve full baskets were collected, and it’s hard not to notice that there were twelve disciples too. Each of those who an hour earlier had said “send them away” went back to the boat carrying his own basket of evidence.

sections.heading: The King Who Slipped Away
paragraphs: The crowd’s reaction is immediate and completely logical: a prophet who feeds people in the wilderness like Moses is a candidate for liberator. John writes that they were about to come and “make Him king by force.” In that century, a scene like this followed a well-worn script: wilderness prophets promising signs like those of Moses gathered huge crowds and ended up as crushed rebels. One of the pretenders after Herod’s death simply put a diadem on his own head. Jesus does the opposite: He withdraws to a mountain by Himself. In the whole Gospel of John the word “king” appears sixteen times, and not once does Jesus say it about Himself. The one title He never used is the very one they will accuse Him of before Pilate a year later. He refused a crown from the hands of the crowd because He had come for a different one: the one we will see woven of thorns a few days from now in our series. The hope He brought was not a political shortcut to a full stomach. It was a longer road, and it reached deeper than the hunger of a single afternoon.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: At the center of this story is a sentence aimed straight at us: “You give them something to eat.” The disciples had excellent arguments that it couldn’t be done: too little money, too little food, too late in the day. Jesus didn’t dispute their math. He asked for what there was, and what there was turned out to be enough, with a surplus that filled twelve baskets. He talks with us the same way when we say our community is too small, the budget too thin and the workers a handful. He doesn’t demand what we don’t have. He asks for the five loaves we do have, truly handed over into His hands. The second thing is the order. Jesus first fed a crowd full of ritually unclean people and postponed the conditions until never. A community that wants to be like Him feeds, welcomes and serves first; it doesn’t set up checkpoints in front of the table. And third: the boy. The only person in this scene who gave Jesus anything was a child with a basket of cheap food. No adult took out a thing. Sometimes the youngest and poorest in a community are holding exactly what God wants to start a miracle with; the question is whether anyone will even ask them what they have.
